claim: PDIA1/P4HB is the most abundant ER oxidoreductase of over 17 members in β cells.
source: In ß cells, protein disulfide isomerase A1 (PDIA1/P4HB), the most abundant ER oxidoreductase of over 17 members, can interact with proinsulin to influence disulfide maturation.
evidence: This claim is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge about the PDI family in the ER.

claim: PDIA1 can interact with proinsulin to influence disulfide maturation.
source: In ß cells, protein disulfide isomerase A1 (PDIA1/P4HB), the most abundant ER oxidoreductase of over 17 members, can interact with proinsulin to influence disulfide maturation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior in vitro studies in the introduction.

claim: Pdia1 is required for optimal insulin production under metabolic stress in vivo.
source: Here we find Pdia1 is required for optimal insulin production under metabolic stress in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the β cell-specific Pdia1 deletion mouse model under HFD conditions.

claim: β cell-specific Pdia1 deletion in young high-fat diet fed mice exacerbated glucose intolerance with inadequate insulinemia.
source: ß cell-specific Pdia1 deletion in young high-fat diet fed mice or aged mice exacerbated glucose intolerance with inadequate insulinemia and increased the proinsulin/insulin ratio in both serum and islets compared to wildtype mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance tests and insulin measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: β cell-specific Pdia1 deletion in aged mice exacerbated glucose intolerance with inadequate insulinemia.
source: ß cell-specific Pdia1 deletion in young high-fat diet fed mice or aged mice exacerbated glucose intolerance with inadequate insulinemia and increased the proinsulin/insulin ratio in both serum and islets compared to wildtype mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance tests in aged mice shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: β cell-specific Pdia1 deletion increased the proinsulin/insulin ratio in both serum and islets compared to wildtype mice.
source: ß cell-specific Pdia1 deletion in young high-fat diet fed mice or aged mice exacerbated glucose intolerance with inadequate insulinemia and increased the proinsulin/insulin ratio in both serum and islets compared to wildtype mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements and Western blot data shown in Figures 3D and 5A-B.

claim: Pdia1-null β cells exhibit diminished insulin granule content.
source: Ultrastructural abnormalities in Pdia1-null ß cells include diminished insulin granule content, ER vesiculation and distention, mitochondrial swelling and nuclear condensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pdia1-null β cells exhibit ER vesiculation and distention.
source: Ultrastructural abnormalities in Pdia1-null ß cells include diminished insulin granule content, ER vesiculation and distention, mitochondrial swelling and nuclear condensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pdia1-null β cells exhibit mitochondrial swelling.
source: Ultrastructural abnormalities in Pdia1-null ß cells include diminished insulin granule content, ER vesiculation and distention, mitochondrial swelling and nuclear condensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pdia1-null β cells exhibit nuclear condensation.
source: Ultrastructural abnormalities in Pdia1-null ß cells include diminished insulin granule content, ER vesiculation and distention, mitochondrial swelling and nuclear condensation.
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4 and nuclear size measurements in Figure 6C.

claim: Pdia1 deletion increased accumulation of disulfide-linked high molecular weight proinsulin complexes.
source: Furthermore, Pdia1 deletion increased accumulation of disulfide-linked high molecular weight proinsulin complexes and islet vulnerability to oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by non-reducing Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Pdia1 deletion increased islet vulnerability to oxidative stress.
source: Furthermore, Pdia1 deletion increased accumulation of disulfide-linked high molecular weight proinsulin complexes and islet vulnerability to oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by menadione treatment experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: PDIA1 contributes to oxidative maturation of proinsulin in the ER to support insulin production and β cell health.
source: These findings demonstrate that PDIA1 contributes to oxidative maturation of proinsulin in the ER to support insulin production and ß cell health.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Type two diabetes mellitus (T2D) is caused by insufficient insulin to meet the level of insulin resistance.
source: Type two diabetes mellitus (T2D) is a complex disease caused by multiple genetic and environmental factors with an overarching problem of insufficient insulin to meet the level of insulin resistance (Mokdad et al., 2001; Sladek et al., 2007; Narayan et al., 2007; Støy et al., 2007; Kaul and Ali, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Pancreatic β cell failure is fundamental in the etiology of T2D.
source: Significant evidence supports the notion that pancreatic ß cell failure is fundamental in the etiology of T2D (Alejandro et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Insulin resistance increases the burden placed on pancreatic β cells to increase insulin synthesis and secretion.
source: Insulin resistance increases the burden placed on pancreatic ß cells to increase insulin synthesis and secretion that leads to associated defects including decreased ß cell number (Clark et al., 1988; Butler et al., 2003; Yoon et al., 2003), chronic ER stress and/or oxidative stress (Robertson et al., 2007; Scheuner and Kaufman, 2008; Back and Kaufman, 2012; Han et al., 2015), and a loss of ß cell identity (Talchai et al., 2012; Swisa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Insulin resistance leads to decreased β cell number.
source: Insulin resistance increases the burden placed on pancreatic ß cells to increase insulin synthesis and secretion that leads to associated defects including decreased ß cell number (Clark et al., 1988; Butler et al., 2003; Yoon et al., 2003), chronic ER stress and/or oxidative stress (Robertson et al., 2007; Scheuner and Kaufman, 2008; Back and Kaufman, 2012; Han et al., 2015), and a loss of ß cell identity (Talchai et al., 2012; Swisa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Insulin resistance leads to chronic ER stress and/or oxidative stress.
source: Insulin resistance increases the burden placed on pancreatic ß cells to increase insulin synthesis and secretion that leads to associated defects including decreased ß cell number (Clark et al., 1988; Butler et al., 2003; Yoon et al., 2003), chronic ER stress and/or oxidative stress (Robertson et al., 2007; Scheuner and Kaufman, 2008; Back and Kaufman, 2012; Han et al., 2015), and a loss of ß cell identity (Talchai et al., 2012; Swisa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Insulin resistance leads to a loss of β cell identity.
source: Insulin resistance increases the burden placed on pancreatic ß cells to increase insulin synthesis and secretion that leads to associated defects including decreased ß cell number (Clark et al., 1988; Butler et al., 2003; Yoon et al., 2003), chronic ER stress and/or oxidative stress (Robertson et al., 2007; Scheuner and Kaufman, 2008; Back and Kaufman, 2012; Han et al., 2015), and a loss of ß cell identity (Talchai et al., 2012; Swisa et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Insulin production is dependent upon differentiation-specific gene expression.
source: Insulin production is dependent upon differentiation-specific gene expression, translation and translocation of preproinsulin into the ER, ER chaperone-facilitated protein folding and disulfide bond formation, vesicular transport of proinsulin from the ER through the Golgi compartments, and stimulus-coupled granule release (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Insulin production is dependent upon translation and translocation of preproinsulin into the ER.
source: Insulin production is dependent upon differentiation-specific gene expression, translation and translocation of preproinsulin into the ER, ER chaperone-facilitated protein folding and disulfide bond formation, vesicular transport of proinsulin from the ER through the Golgi compartments, and stimulus-coupled granule release (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Insulin production is dependent upon ER chaperone-facilitated protein folding and disulfide bond formation.
source: Insulin production is dependent upon differentiation-specific gene expression, translation and translocation of preproinsulin into the ER, ER chaperone-facilitated protein folding and disulfide bond formation, vesicular transport of proinsulin from the ER through the Golgi compartments, and stimulus-coupled granule release (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Insulin production is dependent upon vesicular transport of proinsulin from the ER through the Golgi compartments.
source: Insulin production is dependent upon differentiation-specific gene expression, translation and translocation of preproinsulin into the ER, ER chaperone-facilitated protein folding and disulfide bond formation, vesicular transport of proinsulin from the ER through the Golgi compartments, and stimulus-coupled granule release (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Insulin production is dependent upon stimulus-coupled granule release.
source: Insulin production is dependent upon differentiation-specific gene expression, translation and translocation of preproinsulin into the ER, ER chaperone-facilitated protein folding and disulfide bond formation, vesicular transport of proinsulin from the ER through the Golgi compartments, and stimulus-coupled granule release (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Protein sorting and assembly of proinsulin into nascent granules in the trans Golgi network sets the framework for proteolytic processing of proinsulin and condensation of insulin with zinc.
source: Protein sorting and assembly of proinsulin into nascent granules in the trans Golgi network sets the framework for proteolytic processing of proinsulin and condensation of insulin with zinc to create mature secretory granules that are staged for secretion in response to stimuli (Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Bottlenecks in protein secretion occur at the stages of correct protein folding in the ER.
source: Well characterized bottlenecks in protein secretion occur at the stages of correct protein folding in the ER, anterograde trafficking through the secretory pathway and defective stimulus-coupled granule exocytosis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Bottlenecks in protein secretion occur at anterograde trafficking through the secretory pathway.
source: Well characterized bottlenecks in protein secretion occur at the stages of correct protein folding in the ER, anterograde trafficking through the secretory pathway and defective stimulus-coupled granule exocytosis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Bottlenecks in protein secretion occur at defective stimulus-coupled granule exocytosis.
source: Well characterized bottlenecks in protein secretion occur at the stages of correct protein folding in the ER, anterograde trafficking through the secretory pathway and defective stimulus-coupled granule exocytosis.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Misfolded proteins in the ER can be retro-translocated to the cytosol and degraded via the ubiquitin proteasome system.
source: Misfolded proteins in the ER can be retro-translocated to the cytosol and degraded via the ubiquitin proteasome system (Wu and Rapoport, 2018) and/or autophagy (Loi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Misfolded proteins in the ER can be degraded via autophagy.
source: Misfolded proteins in the ER can be retro-translocated to the cytosol and degraded via the ubiquitin proteasome system (Wu and Rapoport, 2018) and/or autophagy (Loi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) through the ER stress transducers PERK, IRE1, and ATF6.
source: Accumulation of misfolded proteins in the ER activates the unfolded protein response (UPR) through the ER stress transducers PERK, IRE1, and ATF6 to alleviate and adapt to the cellular stress.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Chronic stress from an inability to resolve protein misfolding can compromise cell health.
source: However, chronic stress from an inability to resolve protein misfolding can compromise cell health (Wang and Kaufman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Defects that cause ER protein misfolding or fail to respond when misfolding occurs lead to development of diabetes in rodents and humans.
source: The vitality of ER homeostasis for ß cell health is underscored by the development of diabetes in rodents and humans with defects that either cause ER protein misfolding or fail to respond when misfolding occurs (Back and Kaufman, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Proinsulin forms a native folded structure in the ER by disulfide bond formation comprised of two linkages between the A and B polypeptide chains (A7-B7 and A20-B19) and one in the A chain (A6-A11).
source: Proinsulin forms a native folded structure in the ER by disulfide bond formation comprised of two linkages between the A and B polypeptide chains (A7-B7 and A20-B19) and one in the A chain (A6-A11) (Liu et al., 2018; Dai and Tang, 1996; Jia et al., 2003; Yan et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: Mutations within proinsulin that impact disulfide bond formation cause neonatal diabetes in humans and Akita mice.
source: Mutations within proinsulin that impact disulfide bond formation cause neonatal diabetes in humans and Akita mice, serving as a model of proinsulin misfolding-induced ß cell failure (Støy et al., 2007; Colombo et al., 2008; Riahi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Disulfide bond formation within secretory proteins occurs during the early stages of protein folding as cysteine residues establish proximity to one another.
source: In general, disulfide bond formation within secretory proteins occurs during the early stages of protein folding as cysteine residues establish proximity to one another; however, enzymes can assist catalyzing this process (Bulleid, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: ERO1 transfers oxidizing equivalents from O2 to form disulfide bonds in a large family of ER oxidoreductases.
source: During disulfide bond formation, ER oxidoreductin 1 (ERO1) transfers oxidizing equivalents from O2 to form disulfide bonds in a large family of ER oxidoreductases (Hudson et al., 2015); this process ultimately culminates in the transfer of electrons from sulfhydryls to molecular oxygen.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The ER oxidoreductase family localized to the ER comprises over 17 members in mammals.
source: This oxidoreductase family localized to the ER comprises over 17 members in mammals and each one interacts with specific substrates in a different manner (Jessop et al., 2009; Braakman and Bulleid, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Each ER oxidoreductase interacts with specific substrates in a different manner.
source: This oxidoreductase family localized to the ER comprises over 17 members in mammals and each one interacts with specific substrates in a different manner (Jessop et al., 2009; Braakman and Bulleid, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PDIA1 is the major oxidoreductase located in the ER lumen.
source: Among them, PDIA1, also known as prolyl 4-hydroxylase beta (P4HB), is the major oxidoreductase located in the ER lumen (Ramming and Appenzeller-Herzog, 2012; Benham, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PDI can catalyze oxidation, reduction, and isomerization of disulfide bonds in the ER.
source: Protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) can catalyze oxidation, reduction, and isomerization of disulfide bonds in the ER (Freedman et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: PDI has four domains (a, a', b, and b') with a linker (x) and acidic C-terminal region (c) where a KDEL ER retention signal resides.
source: PDI has four domains (a, a', b, and b') with a linker (x) and acidic C-terminal region (c) where a KDEL ER retention signal resides (Hatahet and Ruddock, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The two catalytic domains of PDI (a, a') are separated by non-catalytic domains (b, b') to form a structure of a-b-b'-x-a'-c.
source: Similar to thioredoxin, the two catalytic domains (a, a') are separated by non-catalytic domains (b, b') to form a structure of a-b-b'-x-a'-c where each catalytic domain has an active site consisting of Cys-Gly-His-Cys residues (Hatahet and Ruddock, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Each catalytic domain of PDI has an active site consisting of Cys-Gly-His-Cys residues.
source: Similar to thioredoxin, the two catalytic domains (a, a') are separated by non-catalytic domains (b, b') to form a structure of a-b-b'-x-a'-c where each catalytic domain has an active site consisting of Cys-Gly-His-Cys residues (Hatahet and Ruddock, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Thiol groups on cysteine residues in the active motif are responsible for the oxidoreductase activity of PDI.
source: Thiol groups on cysteine residues in the active motif are responsible for the oxidoreductase activity, enabling PDI to catalyze both disulfide bond formation as well as disulfide bond isomerization for selective substrates (Hudson et al., 2015; Hatahet and Ruddock, 2007; Freedman, 1995; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PDI exhibits chaperone activity independent of its disulfide isomerase-activity.
source: In addition, PDI also exhibits chaperone activity, independent of its disulfide isomerase-activity as it binds to misfolded proteins to prevent their aggregation (Puig and Gilbert, 1994; Wilson et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PDIA1 catalyzes both disulfide bond formation and isomerization of proinsulin in vitro.
source: Although PDIA1 catalyzes both disulfide bond formation and isomerization of proinsulin in vitro (Winter et al., 2011), it remains unknown how PDIA1 influences proinsulin folding and insulin production in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Therapeutics directed to promote native disulfide bond formation within proinsulin is an attractive strategy to prevent β cell failure in T2D.
source: The results support the conclusion that therapeutics directed to promote native disulfide bond formation within proinsulin is an attractive strategy to prevent ß cell failure in T2D.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: PDIA1 is highly expressed in islets.
source: As PDIA1 is highly expressed in islets (Cras-Méneur et al., 2004; Ahmed and Bergsten, 2005), we pursued analysis of ß cell-specific conditional Pdia1-null mice using tamoxifen (Tam)-regulated deletion of floxed Pdia1 alleles (Kim et al., 2013) through rat insulin promoter driven Cre-recombinase (RIP-CreERT) (Figure 1A) (Dor et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Tamoxifen injection in Pdia1 fl/fl;CreERT mice resulted in ~75% decrease in Pdia1 mRNA in isolated islets.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) demonstrated an ~75% decrease in Pdia1 mRNA in isolated islets from the ß cell-specific Pdia1-knock out mice (Pdia1 fl/fl;CreERT herein, KO, but genotypes are defined in the figures) with no effects on Insulin 2, Pdia6 or Pdia3 mRNAs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Pdia1 deletion had no effects on Insulin 2, Pdia6 or Pdia3 mRNAs.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-PCR) demonstrated an ~75% decrease in Pdia1 mRNA in isolated islets from the ß cell-specific Pdia1-knock out mice (Pdia1 fl/fl;CreERT herein, KO, but genotypes are defined in the figures) with no effects on Insulin 2, Pdia6 or Pdia3 mRNAs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice with or without the RIP-CreERT allele did not show significant differences in glucose homeostasis after a 14 wk HFD.
source: Early studies demonstrated that mice with or without the RIP-CreERT allele did not show significant differences in glucose homeostasis after a 14 wk HFD (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Western blotting of isolated islets from Tam-treated mice with the RIP-CreERT allele demonstrated significantly reduced PDIA1 protein.
source: Western blotting of isolated islets from Tam-treated mice with the RIP-CreERT allele demonstrated significantly reduced PDIA1 protein with increased expression of the UPR genes BiP, PDIA6 and GRP94 (Figure 1C–D), suggesting Pdia1 deletion may cause ER stress in ß cells of the KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Western blotting of isolated islets from Tam-treated mice with the RIP-CreERT allele demonstrated increased expression of the UPR genes BiP, PDIA6 and GRP94.
source: Western blotting of isolated islets from Tam-treated mice with the RIP-CreERT allele demonstrated significantly reduced PDIA1 protein with increased expression of the UPR genes BiP, PDIA6 and GRP94 (Figure 1C–D), suggesting Pdia1 deletion may cause ER stress in ß cells of the KO mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Pdia1 deletion may cause ER stress in β cells of the KO mice.
source: Western blotting of isolated islets from Tam-treated mice with the RIP-CreERT allele demonstrated significantly reduced PDIA1 protein with increased expression of the UPR genes BiP, PDIA6 and GRP94 (Figure 1C–D), suggesting Pdia1 deletion may cause ER stress in ß cells of the KO mice.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the increased expression of UPR genes shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Immunohistochemistry confirmed the absence of PDIA1 in a β cell-specific manner in the KO mice.
source: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) of pancreas tissue sections with antibodies specific for proinsulin/insulin, glucagon and PDIA1 confirmed the absence of PDIA1 in a ß cell-specific manner in the KO mice (Figure 2A–B, compare middle panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Islet α cells express very low levels of PDIA1.
source: Interestingly, analysis of glucagon staining in pancreas sections detected very low PDIA1 expression in islet α cells (Figure 2C, middle panels), and we note that proglucagon contains no disulfide bonds.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Proglucagon contains no disulfide bonds.
source: Interestingly, analysis of glucagon staining in pancreas sections detected very low PDIA1 expression in islet α cells (Figure 2C, middle panels), and we note that proglucagon contains no disulfide bonds.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the structure of proglucagon.

claim: The RIP-CreERT allele was reported to be expressed in the hypothalamus.
source: Although the RIP-CreERT allele was reported to be expressed in the hypothalamus (Wicksteed et al., 2010), Western blotting of PDIA1 in hypothalamic tissue did not detect reduced PDIA1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Western blotting of PDIA1 in hypothalamic tissue did not detect reduced PDIA1 expression in KO mice.
source: Although the RIP-CreERT allele was reported to be expressed in the hypothalamus (Wicksteed et al., 2010), Western blotting of PDIA1 in hypothalamic tissue did not detect reduced PDIA1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The RIP-CreERT allele did not affect serum dopamine.
source: In addition, we previously reported that this RIP-CreERT allele did not affect serum dopamine, which is synthesized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (Hahm et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Dopamine is synthesized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus.
source: In addition, we previously reported that this RIP-CreERT allele did not affect serum dopamine, which is synthesized in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus (Hahm et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and supported by a citation.

claim: There was no difference in expression of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) in the KO mice compared to the control genotypes with the RIP-CreERT allele.
source: Although we detected Cre positive staining in the hypothalamus, there was no difference in expression of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) in the KO mice compared to the control genotypes with the RIP-CreERT allele.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations by the authors.

claim: Young male and female mice did not exhibit any defects in glucose homeostasis.
source: Young male and female mice did not exhibit any defects in glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations by the authors.

claim: On a regular chow diet, the challenge of aging in KO males caused statistically significant increase in glucose intolerance.
source: However, on a regular chow diet, the challenge of aging in KO males caused statistically significant increase in glucose intolerance (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Genetic controls (Pdia1 fl/fl and fl/+) and KO mice fed HFD up to 32 wks showed no significant differences in body weight or weight gain.
source: Genetic controls (Pdia1 fl/fl and fl/+) and KO mice fed HFD up to 32 wks showed no significant differences in body weight or weight gain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Fasting blood glucose (4 hr) in the HFD mice was significantly elevated in the KO versus genetic controls.
source: However, fasting blood glucose (4 hr) in the HFD mice was significantly elevated in the KO versus genetic controls (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fasting blood glucose measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Glucose intolerance was observed in HFD-fed KO mice as measured by the difference in the area under the glucose excursion curve (Delta-AUC).
source: In addition, glucose intolerance was observed in HFD-fed KO mice as measured by the difference in the area under the glucose excursion curve (Delta-AUC) (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by glucose tolerance test data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Serum insulin levels were decreased in HFD-fed KO mice.
source: Serum insulin levels were decreased in HFD-fed KO mice, and a fasting-refeeding challenge revealed hypoinsulinemia with an increased proinsulin/insulin ratio (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A fasting-refeeding challenge revealed hypoinsulinemia with an increased proinsulin/insulin ratio in HFD-fed KO mice.
source: Serum insulin levels were decreased in HFD-fed KO mice, and a fasting-refeeding challenge revealed hypoinsulinemia with an increased proinsulin/insulin ratio (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Pdia1 deletion did not affect insulin sensitivity measured by insulin tolerance tests.
source: Pdia1 deletion did not affect insulin sensitivity measured by insulin tolerance tests (Figure 3E) and no significant difference was observed in the percent of ß cell area to total pancreas or ß cell area per islet in HFD-fed KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by insulin tolerance test data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: No significant difference was observed in the percent of β cell area to total pancreas or β cell area per islet in HFD-fed KO mice.
source: Pdia1 deletion did not affect insulin sensitivity measured by insulin tolerance tests (Figure 3E) and no significant difference was observed in the percent of ß cell area to total pancreas or ß cell area per islet in HFD-fed KO mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the setting of metabolic challenge, Pdia1 is required for adequate insulin production to maintain systemic glucose homeostasis.
source: These results indicate that in the setting of metabolic challenge, Pdia1 is required for adequate insulin production to maintain systemic glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Pdia1 deletion did not significantly decrease β cell- and α cell- specific mRNAs.
source: The results demonstrated no significant decrease in ß cell- and α cell- specific mRNAs, mRNAs encoding the insulin processing enzymes PC1/3, PC2, and CPE, or mRNAs encoding ß cell transcription factors PDX1 or MAFA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Pdia1 deletion did not significantly decrease mRNAs encoding the insulin processing enzymes PC1/3, PC2, and CPE.
source: The results demonstrated no significant decrease in ß cell- and α cell- specific mRNAs, mRNAs encoding the insulin processing enzymes PC1/3, PC2, and CPE, or mRNAs encoding ß cell transcription factors PDX1 or MAFA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Pdia1 deletion did not significantly decrease mRNAs encoding β cell transcription factors PDX1 or MAFA.
source: The results demonstrated no significant decrease in ß cell- and α cell- specific mRNAs, mRNAs encoding the insulin processing enzymes PC1/3, PC2, and CPE, or mRNAs encoding ß cell transcription factors PDX1 or MAFA (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The reduced insulin content in KO serum and islets was not due to reduced β cell-specific gene expression.
source: Therefore, the reduced insulin content in KO serum and islets (Figure 3D) was not due to reduced ß cell-specific gene expression.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There was no significant change in expression of other PDI family members and Serca2b, except for Pdia4.
source: There was also no significant change in expression of other PDI family members and Serca2b, except for Pdia4 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: UPR genes were not significantly elevated in the Pdia1 KO islets, other than Grp94.
source: In addition, UPR genes were not significantly elevated at this point in time in the Pdia1 KO islets, other than Grp94 (Figure 3H), which correlated with a slight increase in protein (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: There were no significant differences in expression of a panel of genes representing the antioxidant response and cell death.
source: Lastly, there were no significant differences in expression of a panel of genes representing the antioxidant response and cell death (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: β cell-specific Pdia1 deletion does not alter expression of β cell specific genes, antioxidant response genes, or cell death genes.
source: These results show that ß cell-specific Pdia1 deletion does not alter expression of ß cell specific genes, antioxidant response genes, or cell death genes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3F-I.

claim: TEM did not detect any significant morphological alterations in the cohorts of KO mice fed a regular diet for 10 wks after Tam injection.
source: TEM did not detect any significant morphological alterations in the cohorts of KO mice fed a regular diet for 10 wks after Tam injection (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations by the authors.

claim: β cells from HFD-fed KO mice showed significant abnormalities including ER vesiculation and distension, mitochondrial swelling, and nuclear condensation.
source: Strikingly however, ß cells from HFD-fed KO mice showed significant abnormalities including ER vesiculation and distension, mitochondrial swelling, and nuclear condensation, that were not observed in genetic control mice (Pdia1 fl/fl and fl/+) (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 4.

claim: KO mice had fewer mature (~15%) and immature (~50%) granules compared to the control genotypes fl/fl and fl/+.
source: To determine whether Pdia1 deletion also affects insulin granule content, we quantified the number of mature (dense dark core, yellow arrows in enlarged image) and immature (inner gray core, orange filled open arrowheads in enlarged image) granules and discovered that KO mice had fewer mature (~15%) and immature (~50%) granules compared to the control genotypes fl/fl and fl/+ (Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of granules from TEM images shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The average cross-sectional area of mature granules in KO mice was 20% larger than control genotypes.
source: Analysis of the cross-sectioned mature granule (MG) vesicle area and dense core size demonstrated that the average cross-sectional area of MGs in KO mice was 20% larger than control genotypes (Figure 4J), however, there was no difference in MG dense core size between genotypes (Figure 4J), suggesting that insulin packaging efficiency within granules was decreased in Pdia1 deleted-ß cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of granule size from TEM images shown in Figure 4J.

claim: There was no difference in mature granule dense core size between genotypes.
source: Analysis of the cross-sectioned mature granule (MG) vesicle area and dense core size demonstrated that the average cross-sectional area of MGs in KO mice was 20% larger than control genotypes (Figure 4J), however, there was no difference in MG dense core size between genotypes (Figure 4J), suggesting that insulin packaging efficiency within granules was decreased in Pdia1 deleted-ß cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of granule size from TEM images shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Insulin packaging efficiency within granules was decreased in Pdia1 deleted-β cells.
source: Analysis of the cross-sectioned mature granule (MG) vesicle area and dense core size demonstrated that the average cross-sectional area of MGs in KO mice was 20% larger than control genotypes (Figure 4J), however, there was no difference in MG dense core size between genotypes (Figure 4J), suggesting that insulin packaging efficiency within granules was decreased in Pdia1 deleted-ß cells.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the granule size data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Pdia1 is essential to maintain β cell ultrastructure upon metabolic stress.
source: Taken together, the findings indicate that Pdia1 is essential to maintain ß cell ultrastructure upon metabolic stress, indicative of suboptimal ß cell function.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the TEM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Insulin levels were lower in KO islets compared to control genotypes.
source: Insulin levels were lower in KO islets compared to control genotypes while the proinsulin/insulin ratio was significantly elevated (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The proinsulin/insulin ratio was significantly elevated in KO islets compared to control genotypes.
source: Insulin levels were lower in KO islets compared to control genotypes while the proinsulin/insulin ratio was significantly elevated (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: BiP/Hspa5 was induced with increased PDIA4 and PDIA6 in Pdia1-deleted versus Pdia1-sufficient islets.
source: BiP/Hspa5 was induced with increased PDIA4 and PDIA6 in Pdia1-deleted versus Pdia1-sufficient islets (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: The increased levels of BiP are consistent with the notion that the absence of Pdia1 causes a mild ER stress.
source: The increased levels of BiP are consistent with the notion that the absence of Pdia1 causes a mild ER stress, suggestive of protein misfolding, which is also consistent with ER distension (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the Western blot data in Figure 5A-B and TEM data in Figure 4.

claim: Western blot analysis under non-reducing conditions demonstrated the appearance of multiple proinsulin bands including a monomer at ~6 kDa and a ladder of molecular masses that could correspond to proinsulin dimers up to pentamers (b, 14–49 kDa) as well as a cluster of HMW complexes (a, 49–198 kDa).
source: Western blot analysis under non-reducing conditions using the CCI-17 antibody demonstrated the appearance of multiple proinsulin bands including a monomer at ~6 kDa (black arrowhead, Figure 5C) and a ladder of molecular masses that could correspond to proinsulin dimers up to pentamers (b, 14–49 kDa) as well as a cluster of HMW complexes (a, 49–198 kDa) in Pdia1 fl/fl and KO islets (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by non-reducing Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Pdia1 deletion increased the amount of HMW complexes relative to the oligomeric forms and decreased the oligomers relative to monomeric proinsulin compared to the genetic controls without the RIP-CreERT allele.
source: Pdia1 deletion increased the amount of HMW complexes relative to the oligomeric forms and decreased the oligomers relative to monomeric proinsulin compared to the genetic controls without the RIP-CreERT allele (Figure 5C, quantified in graph).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of non-reducing Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The epitope reactivity of the CCI-17 monoclonal antibody is very dependent on the status of proinsulin sulfhydryls and disulfide bonds.
source: During the course of our studies we discovered that the epitope reactivity of the CCI-17 monoclonal antibody is very dependent the status of proinsulin sulfhydryls and disulfide bonds.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations by the authors.

claim: When the non-reducing SDS-PAGE gel was treated with dithiothreitol (DTT) prior to transfer to nitrocellulose, there was a great increase in antibody reactivity with monomeric proinsulin.
source: First, when the non-reducing SDS-PAGE gel was treated with dithiothreitol (DTT) prior to transfer to nitrocellulose, we observed a great increase in antibody reactivity with monomeric proinsulin (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Opening the proinsulin molecule significantly enhances epitope exposure to the CCI-17 antibody.
source: This suggests that opening the proinsulin molecule significantly enhances epitope exposure to the CCI-17 antibody.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the DTT treatment experiment shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Western blotting analysis of the non-reducing SDS-PAGE gel demonstrated readily detectable proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes in WT murine islets, nondiabetic human islets and in prediabetic db/db islets prior to onset of hyperglycemia.
source: It is also important to note that Western blotting analysis of the non-reducing SDS-PAGE gel (with or without subsequent DTT treatment of the gel prior to transfer) demonstrated readily detectable proinsulin disulfide-linked complexes in WT murine islets, nondiabetic human islets and in prediabetic db/db islets prior to onset of hyperglycemia (Arunagiri et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a complementary study.

claim: Treatment with N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) to alkylate free sulfhydryls slightly increased the HMW proinsulin-containing complexes and slightly reduced the disulfide-linked oligomers.
source: The second finding is that treatment with N-ethylmaleimide (NEM) to alkylate free sulfhydryls slightly increased the HMW proinsulin-containing complexes and slightly reduced the disulfide-linked oligomers (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PDIA1 may be required to reduce the HMW complexes and NEM treatment inactivates PDIA1, thereby stabilizing the HMW complexes.
source: We suggest that PDIA1 may be required to reduce the HMW complexes and NEM treatment inactivates PDIA1, thereby stabilizing the HMW complexes.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the NEM treatment experiment shown in Figure 5E.

claim: DTT treatment of islets produced increasing amounts of the proinsulin monomer and residual disulfide-linked dimer.
source: To gain further insight into the nature of the disulfide-linked oligomers, islets isolated from WT male mice fed a regular diet were treated in culture with increasing concentrations of dithiothreitol (DTT) to increase the ER reduction potential. This treatment produced increasing amounts of the proinsulin monomer and residual disulfide-linked dimer (Figure 5F), consistent with findings of Arunagiri et al. (2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Female KO mice fed a regular diet for 14 wks after Tam also showed increased HMW complexes relative to the disulfide-linked proinsulin oligomers and reduced oligomers relative to monomeric proinsulin compared to the genetic controls.
source: In addition, female KO mice fed a regular diet for 14 wks after Tam also showed increased HMW complexes relative to the disulfide-linked proinsulin oligomers and reduced oligomers relative to monomeric proinsulin compared to the genetic controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Menadione treatment significantly increased ROS in islets.
source: Menadione treatment significantly increased ROS as observed by CellROX Deep Red stain (Figure 6A) and ß cells with Pdia1 deletion showed greater ROS accumulation than those of genetic control fl/+ islets (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROS staining data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: β cells with Pdia1 deletion showed greater ROS accumulation than those of genetic control fl/+ islets.
source: Menadione treatment significantly increased ROS as observed by CellROX Deep Red stain (Figure 6A) and ß cells with Pdia1 deletion showed greater ROS accumulation than those of genetic control fl/+ islets (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by ROS staining data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Menadione promoted nuclear condensation.
source: Furthermore, both the average size and the histogram-analyzed nuclear size after Hoechst 33342 staining demonstrated that menadione promoted nuclear condensation (Figure 6C) and this effect appeared to be greater in KO islets compared to the genetic controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear size measurements shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: The effect of menadione on nuclear condensation appeared to be greater in KO islets compared to the genetic controls.
source: Furthermore, both the average size and the histogram-analyzed nuclear size after Hoechst 33342 staining demonstrated that menadione promoted nuclear condensation (Figure 6C) and this effect appeared to be greater in KO islets compared to the genetic controls (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by nuclear size measurements shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: In the absence of menadione treatment, Pdia1 deletion increased the HMW proinsulin complexes (a, 49–198 kDa) compared to WT islets.
source: Consistently, in the absence of menadione treatment, Pdia1 deletion increased the HMW proinsulin complexes (a, 49–198 kDa) compared to WT islets, and this effect was even greater in islets treated with menadione (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The effect of Pdia1 deletion on HMW proinsulin complexes was even greater in islets treated with menadione.
source: Consistently, in the absence of menadione treatment, Pdia1 deletion increased the HMW proinsulin complexes (a, 49–198 kDa) compared to WT islets, and this effect was even greater in islets treated with menadione (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: DTT treatment of the gel prior to nitrocellulose transfer demonstrated no difference between untreated and NEM-treated islets.
source: Importantly, DTT treatment of the gel prior to nitrocellulose transfer demonstrated no difference between untreated and NEM-treated islets (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: β cells lacking Pdia1 are more sensitive to oxidizing conditions that promote the formation of HMW proinsulin complexes.
source: Taken together, these results show that ß cells lacking Pdia1 are more sensitive to oxidizing conditions that promote the formation of HMW proinsulin complexes.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the menadione treatment experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: BFA treatment significantly increased proinsulin complex formation.
source: BFA treatment significantly increased proinsulin complex formation, thus supporting the notion that the aberrant multimers/HMW complexes are a consequence of increased proinsulin content in the ER (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The aberrant multimers/HMW complexes are a consequence of increased proinsulin content in the ER.
source: BFA treatment significantly increased proinsulin complex formation, thus supporting the notion that the aberrant multimers/HMW complexes are a consequence of increased proinsulin content in the ER (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the BFA treatment experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Treatment with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX) did not significantly affect the results, other than an expected reduced proinsulin content.
source: Treatment with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), did not significantly affect the results, other than an expected reduced proinsulin content, indicating the presynthesized proinsulin is subject to multimer/HMW complex formation when its abundance in the ER is increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Presynthesized proinsulin is subject to multimer/HMW complex formation when its abundance in the ER is increased.
source: Treatment with the translation elongation inhibitor cycloheximide (CHX), did not significantly affect the results, other than an expected reduced proinsulin content, indicating the presynthesized proinsulin is subject to multimer/HMW complex formation when its abundance in the ER is increased.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the CHX treatment experiment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Infection with Ad-hProins produced significant amounts of reduced and oxidized proinsulin upon analysis by non-reducing SDS-PAGE with DTT treatment prior to transfer to nitrocellulose.
source: Infection with Ad-hProins produced significant amounts of reduced and oxidized proinsulin upon analysis by non-reducing SDS-PAGE with DTT treatment prior to transfer to nitrocellulose (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Treatment of cells with increasing concentrations of DTT increased the amount of reduced proinsulin.
source: Treatment of cells with increasing concentrations of DTT increased the amount of reduced proinsulin (lanes 3,4), as expected.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Forced expression of PDIA1, but not catalytically inactive PDIA1, increased the amount of reduced proinsulin.
source: Significantly, forced expression of PDIA1, but not catalytically inactive PDIA1, increased the amount of reduced proinsulin (lanes 5, 6, 8, 10 and 12).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: PDIA1 acts as a reductase to prevent aberrant proinsulin oxidation.
source: Therefore, the results support the hypothesis that PDIA1 acts as a reductase to prevent aberrant proinsulin oxidation, consistent with previous studies in vitro (Rajpal et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3 and is supported by a citation to previous in vitro studies.

claim: The KSC-34 inhibitor alone slightly increased HMW complexes.
source: The results show that the KSC-34 inhibitor alone slightly increased HMW complexes.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When combined with menadione, KSC-34 treatment recapitulated the effect of Pdia1 deletion upon menadione treatment.
source: However, when combined with menadione, KSC-34 treatment recapitulated the effect of Pdia1 deletion upon menadione treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Either a PDIA1 chemical inhibitor or gene deletion exhibit similar effects on the generation of HMW complexes, especially upon oxidant treatment.
source: Importantly, the findings demonstrate that either a PDIA1 chemical inhibitor or gene deletion exhibit similar effects on the generation of HMW complexes, especially upon oxidant treatment.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the KSC-34 inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: PDIA1 is increasingly important for insulin production in the face of either age or metabolic stress imposed by a HFD.
source: PDIA1 is the major ER oxidoreductase in the majority of mammalian cells, including ß cells. Although numerous in vitro studies demonstrated that PDI actively engages proinsulin to catalyze disulfide bond formation (Winter et al., 2011; Rajpal et al., 2012; Winter et al., 2002; Wright et al., 2013), there is little information regarding the significance of PDI action in vivo. Here, using ß cell specific Pdia1 deletion we show that PDIA1 is increasingly important for insulin production in the face of either age or metabolic stress imposed by a HFD.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main findings from the in vivo experiments.

claim: When compromised by HFD feeding, mice with β cell-specific Pdia1 deletion displayed exaggerated glucose intolerance with significant β cell abnormalities.
source: Specifically, when compromised by HFD feeding, mice with ß cell-specific Pdia1 deletion displayed exaggerated glucose intolerance with significant ß cell abnormalities including diminished islet and serum insulin accompanied by an increased proinsulin/insulin ratio in islets and serum (Figure 3), with diminished insulin packaging and storage in secretory granules and a reduced number of insulin secretory granules (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the findings shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: β cell Pdia1 deletion caused abnormal ultrastructural changes including ER distension and vesiculation, mitochondrial swelling, and nuclear condensation.
source: In addition, ß cell Pdia1 deletion caused abnormal ultrastructural changes including ER distension and vesiculation, mitochondrial swelling, and nuclear condensation (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Pdia1-deleted islets were sensitive to oxidant challenge.
source: Pdia1-deleted islets were also sensitive to oxidant challenge (Figure 6), which is significant because PDIA1 is a highly abundant ER protein (~mM concentration [Freedman et al., 1994]) that is primarily in a reduced form (Hudson et al., 2015) and although it cycles, it may significantly contribute to redox homeostasis in the ER.
evidence: This claim is supported by menadione treatment experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: PDIA1 is a highly abundant ER protein (~mM concentration).
source: Pdia1-deleted islets were also sensitive to oxidant challenge (Figure 6), which is significant because PDIA1 is a highly abundant ER protein (~mM concentration [Freedman et al., 1994]) that is primarily in a reduced form (Hudson et al., 2015) and although it cycles, it may significantly contribute to redox homeostasis in the ER.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: PDIA1 is primarily in a reduced form.
source: Pdia1-deleted islets were also sensitive to oxidant challenge (Figure 6), which is significant because PDIA1 is a highly abundant ER protein (~mM concentration [Freedman et al., 1994]) that is primarily in a reduced form (Hudson et al., 2015) and although it cycles, it may significantly contribute to redox homeostasis in the ER.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: PDIA1 may significantly contribute to redox homeostasis in the ER.
source: Pdia1-deleted islets were also sensitive to oxidant challenge (Figure 6), which is significant because PDIA1 is a highly abundant ER protein (~mM concentration [Freedman et al., 1994]) that is primarily in a reduced form (Hudson et al., 2015) and although it cycles, it may significantly contribute to redox homeostasis in the ER.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the properties of PDIA1 and the experimental results.

claim: PDI can reduce improper proinsulin disulfide bonds as demonstrated during infection with pathogens that require reduction for retro-translocation from the ER to the cytosol.
source: Alternatively, PDIA1 may reduce improper proinsulin disulfide bonds as demonstrated during infection with pathogens that require reduction for retro-translocation from the ER to the cytosol (Tsai et al., 2001; Inoue et al., 2015) and from evidence that supports a role for PDI as a reductase important for degradation of mutant Akita proinsulin (He et al., 2015) and mutant thyroglobulin (Forster et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: PDI acts as a reductase important for degradation of mutant Akita proinsulin.
source: Alternatively, PDIA1 may reduce improper proinsulin disulfide bonds as demonstrated during infection with pathogens that require reduction for retro-translocation from the ER to the cytosol (Tsai et al., 2001; Inoue et al., 2015) and from evidence that supports a role for PDI as a reductase important for degradation of mutant Akita proinsulin (He et al., 2015) and mutant thyroglobulin (Forster et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: PDI acts as a reductase important for degradation of mutant thyroglobulin.
source: Alternatively, PDIA1 may reduce improper proinsulin disulfide bonds as demonstrated during infection with pathogens that require reduction for retro-translocation from the ER to the cytosol (Tsai et al., 2001; Inoue et al., 2015) and from evidence that supports a role for PDI as a reductase important for degradation of mutant Akita proinsulin (He et al., 2015) and mutant thyroglobulin (Forster et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Proinsulin disulfide maturation in the ER is absolutely required for proinsulin export to the Golgi complex for delivery to immature granules.
source: Proinsulin disulfide maturation in the ER is absolutely required for proinsulin export to the Golgi complex for delivery to immature granules (Haataja et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The identification of mutations in the INS gene coding sequence increased our understanding how proinsulin misfolding contributes to the development of β cell failure and diabetes.
source: The identification of mutations in the INS gene coding sequence increased our understanding how proinsulin misfolding contributes to the development of ß cell failure and diabetes (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Based on the greater accumulation of HMW disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes in Pdia1-null islets, the data strongly suggest that PDIA1 participates in the resolution/dissolution of these inappropriate disulfide-linked complexes.
source: If PDIA1 assists in disulfide isomerization to facilitate correct disulfide bonding in proinsulin, its absence could increase aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes, which we observed in Pdia1-deleted islets (Figure 5). Although the role of PDIA1 in vivo is complicated by the presence of other ER oxidoreductases and glutathione, based on the greater accumulation of HMW disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes in Pdia1-null islets, the data strongly suggest that PDIA1 participates in the resolution/dissolution of these inappropriate disulfide-linked complexes (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: PDIA1 resolution/dissolution of inappropriate disulfide-linked complexes could include both PDI chaperone function as well as oxidoreductase function.
source: This could include both PDI chaperone function as well as oxidoreductase function.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the mechanism of PDIA1 action.

claim: Healthy murine WT islets exhibit a lower level of HMW complexes in addition to smaller oligomeric disulfide-linked proinsulin species.
source: It is important to note that healthy murine WT islets also exhibit a lower level of these HMW complexes in addition to smaller oligomeric disulfide-linked proinsulin species (Arunagiri et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a complementary study.

claim: The increased BiP expression in the islets bearing Pdia1-deleted β cells suggests that increased accumulation of inappropriate disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes may induce ER stress.
source: Importantly, the increased BiP expression in the islets bearing Pdia1-deleted ß cells suggests that increased accumulation of inappropriate disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes may induce ER stress, supporting a link between aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes and a compromise in ß cell health and function.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the Western blot data showing increased BiP expression in Figure 5A-B.

claim: There is a link between aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes and a compromise in β cell health and function.
source: Importantly, the increased BiP expression in the islets bearing Pdia1-deleted ß cells suggests that increased accumulation of inappropriate disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes may induce ER stress, supporting a link between aberrant disulfide-linked proinsulin complexes and a compromise in ß cell health and function.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: PDIA1 is not required but increases the efficiency of proinsulin maturation, possibly by reducing HMW proinsulin complexes.
source: Here, we show that PDIA1 is not required but increases the efficiency of proinsulin maturation, possibly by reducing HMW proinsulin complexes.
evidence: This claim is stated in Figure 7 and is a summary of the main findings.

claim: In the absence of PDIA1, disulfide bond formation, reduction and/or isomerization in proinsulin are inadequate during increased demand so HMW proinsulin complexes accumulate in the ER upon metabolic pressure, such as a HFD.
source: In the absence of PDIA1, disulfide bond formation, reduction and/or isomerization in proinsulin are inadequate during increased demand so HMW proinsulin complexes accumulate in the ER upon metabolic pressure, such as a HFD.
evidence: This claim is stated in Figure 7 and is a summary of the main findings.

claim: PDIA1 optimizes proinsulin maturation needed for insulin biosynthesis and for the maintenance of normoglycemia under conditions of metabolic stress in vivo.
source: Based on our results, we conclude that PDIA1 optimizes proinsulin maturation needed for insulin biosynthesis and for the maintenance of normoglycemia under conditions of metabolic stress in vivo.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings should open a new field of investigation to elucidate how the PDI family members impact oxidative protein folding and redox homeostasis in the ER of pancreatic β cells.
source: Our findings should open a new field of investigation to elucidate how the PDI family members impact oxidative protein folding and redox homeostasis in the ER of pancreatic ß cells, as well as provide a fundamental basis to understand how protein folding is essential to protect ß cells from collapse, contributing to the onset of T2D.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The findings provide a fundamental basis to understand how protein folding is essential to protect β cells from collapse, contributing to the onset of T2D.
